column1: # Saved agent rules that let an agent run commands on another machine without asking. Two kinds of
# line, tab separated. After editing, run: bash tools/gen.sh
#   cmd   words  case  label  source
#     words   a command that runs commands on another machine, as the words it starts with
#     case    exact, or any for a command its shell reads without case (PowerShell's cmdlets)
#     label   where the commands it runs run, as the report shows it after "runs commands"
#     source  the vendor's page that says the command runs commands on another machine
#   file  agent  os  format  group  path  note
#     agent   as the report shows it
#     os      all, mac, linux or win (win is Git Bash and gird-check.ps1)
#     format  how the file's rules are read (below)
#     group   agent: a deny or ask rule in any file of that agent's lines can override an allow
#             rule in another; file: only one in the same file
#     path    the file, with the path tokens data/sessions.tsv uses. One folder may be *, for that
#             file in every folder there (VS Code keeps a settings file for each profile), or the
#             file name may be *.ext, for every such file in that folder
#     note    added to the report's line, or -
# A rule is read as the words it fixes before its first wildcard. It hits a cmd line when those words
# and the line's words agree as far as the shorter goes: aws, ssh prod-1 and aws ssm send-command all
# hit; aws s3, ssh-keygen and git do not. A wildcard glued to a word (ssh*) covers any word it starts.
# A rule with no wildcard is that exact command, and hits only when it has more words than the line:
# Bash(ssh prod-1 uptime) runs uptime on prod-1, while Bash(ssh) or Bash(kubectl exec) alone runs no
# command elsewhere. Whether the words past the command name a host and a command is not checked, so
# Bash(ssh prod-1), a login with no command, also hits. A rule shorter than the line (Bash(aws *)) is
# reported as allowing every such command. A deny or ask rule drops the hit only when it covers every
# use of the line's command (its words, then any text, with nothing after its wildcard: Bash(ssh * rm)
# or Bash(* --force) covers none) and the agent would apply it over the allow rule. A regex rule is
# shown as written, up to a run of 16 letters or digits and to 64 characters. Limits: a rule that puts other words first
# (aws --region x ssm send-command) is not caught, and neither is a regex that starts with a group or a
# class ((ssh|scp) .*). A rule that allows every command (Bash, or a tool allowed whole) is not
# reported here: section 1 reports Claude Code's above this list.
# Formats, with the source each reader follows:
#   claude  Claude Code settings, permissions.allow, ask and deny, rules Bash(...) and PowerShell(...)
#           (code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): deny, then ask, then allow, and a deny or ask
#           from any file wins; * matches any text, a space before a trailing * also matches the bare
#           command, :* at the end is the same as a trailing space and *, and PowerShell rules match
#           without case. Managed settings are not read. A project's .claude/settings.local.json
#           applies without trusting the folder, and is read for every project the home scan finds;
#           a project's .claude/settings.json allow rules wait for that trust, and section 2 lists them.
#   codex   Codex .rules files, prefix_rule(pattern=[...], decision=...) (openai/codex at c764c44:
#           codex-rs/execpolicy/README.md, amend.rs writes one rule a line on "always allow",
#           core/src/exec_policy.rs reads every *.rules file in rules/ of each config folder). Tokens
#           match the command's first words in order; a list is alternatives; allow, prompt (ask) and
#           forbidden (deny), the strictest wins. A project's .codex/rules load only once the
#           project is trusted (config/src/loader/mod.rs) and are not read here.
#   gemini-toml  Gemini CLI policy files, [[rule]] with toolName run_shell_command, commandPrefix
#           (a string or a list) or commandRegex, decision allow, deny or ask_user, and priority
#           (google-gemini/gemini-cli at 615d6bc: docs/reference/policy-engine.md,
#           packages/core/src/policy/toml-loader.ts and utils.ts). A prefix ends at a space or the
#           command's end; a regex is matched from the command's start. The highest priority wins:
#           a user file's rule counts as 4 plus its priority over 1000 (config.ts); a deny or ask of
#           the same priority is read as winning. A rule with argsPattern is not read. A rule with
#           modes applies only in them: one without default is reported with its modes, a deny or ask
#           one covers nothing, and an allow for yolo alone is not reported, as yolo mode runs every
#           command without asking anyway.
#   gemini-json  Gemini CLI settings.json tools.allowed (run_shell_command(prefix), at 4.3, and with
#           one a deny of every other command at 4.29), tools.core (allows at 4.25, a deny of every
#           other tool at 4.24), tools.confirmationRequired (ask, 4.35) and tools.exclude (deny, 4.4)
#           of the shell tool (packages/core/src/policy/config.ts).
#   vscode  VS Code chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove (microsoft/vscode at 22d53a1ff:
#           terminalChatAgentToolsConfiguration.ts and commandLineAutoApprover.ts). A key matches the
#           start of a command up to a word boundary, or is a /regex/ with flags; true approves, false
#           always asks and wins over true, and an object's approve does the same. It declares no
#           scope, so a profile's settings file holds its own.
#   roo     Roo Code roo-cline.allowedCommands and deniedCommands in VS Code's user settings
#           (RooCodeInc/Roo-Code at b867ec9: src/package.json, src/core/auto-approval/commands.ts).
#           A command is allowed when it starts with an entry, without case and with no word boundary;
#           the longest matching entry of either list wins, a tie to the denied one. Roo Code applies
#           them only while its auto-approve for commands is on, which it keeps outside these files.
#   amazonq Amazon Q Developer CLI agent files, toolsSettings.execute_bash (execute_cmd on Windows)
#           allowedCommands and deniedCommands (aws/amazon-q-developer-cli at 15cc8f3:
#           docs/built-in-tools.md, crates/chat-cli/src/cli/chat/tools/execute/mod.rs): each is a regex
#           of the whole command, and a denied match wins. Global agents are in ~/.aws/amazonq/cli-agents
#           (crates/chat-cli/src/util/paths.rs).
